Missing Texas State student’s remains identified after nearly six years

Missing Texas State student’s remains identified after nearly six years

Foster Conner, News Contributor
September 28, 2026
Aiden Fritsche
Texas State fans hold a moment of silence, Saturday, Sept. 26, at UFCU Stadium. The moment of silence was in memory of Jason Landry.
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 3:18
Instaread

Six years after Texas State student Jason Landry disappeared, DNA testing has confirmed that recently recovered remains in Caldwell County belong to him.

Landry, who was 21, went missing while driving back to his home in Missouri City, Texas. On Dec. 13, 2020, his 2003 Nissan Altima was discovered on Salt Flat Road near Luling, Texas, alongside some personal belongings; however, his body was not recovered.

On Sept. 23, the Attorney General’s Office announced in a press release that skeletal remains discovered on Sept. 8 east of Salt Flat Road, between Soda Springs and Biggs Road, had been identified as those of Landry. The location was in proximity to the crash site, according to a Caldwell County press release.

The University of North Texas’ Center for Human Identification conducted the DNA testing, however, according to officials, the recovered remains did not yield sufficient evidence to determine the cause or manner of death. Investigators reported that there was no evidence indicating foul play.

In an email to The Star, Jayme Blaschke, director of university communications and public relations, wrote that the university community was saddened by the identification and expressed support for Landry’s family, friends and classmates.

“Our hearts are with them as they grieve this loss,” Blaschke wrote. “University counseling and support resources are available to students, faculty and staff members who may need them during this time.”

The Forensic Anthropology Center at Texas State (FACTS) also assisted with the search and recovery. Blaschke wrote that FACTS was on-site in Caldwell County Sept. 10 to assist with the recovery of Landry’s remains.

According to the email, FACTS’ faculty, staff and students provided technical and scientific assistance throughout the search, including training, skeletal consultation, drone imaging and field search and recovery. The center worked with the Caldwell County Sheriff’s Office, Texas Rangers, Texas Search and Rescue (TEXSAR) and civilian search teams.

“We are proud to have been a part of the mission to bring Jason home and our thoughts are with his family at this time,” FACTS wrote in an email to
The Star.

Landry’s disappearance has remained on the mind’s of the Texas State community with annual vigils held by his family, volunteers from around the community conducting searches for Landry and special shirts worn during events for Landry.

Donna Egenolf, Landry’s aunt, said in a previous interview with The Star that during the candlelit vigil held for Landry on the fifth anniversary of his disappearance that members of the Jason Landry Search Team wore bright yellow shirts with “Bring Jason home soon” on the front.

“I notice everybody’s in their bright yellow [Landry] shirts, and I love it,” Egenolf said. “When I was asked to speak with an intro, this is what came to mind, so I am going to go with it. One of the songs that was Jason’s favorite was “Waymaker” song by Michael W. Smith, and you can see it’s on our shirts.

During the vigil, Kent Landry, Jason’s father, spoke about the impact of his son’s disappearance on the family, while other family members and friends shared memories of Jason.

During the Sept. 26, 2026 Texas State Football game against Incarnate Word, the university held a moment of silence for Landry before the national anthem.

Kent Landry said he was surprised by Texas State honoring his son at the football game.

“He was only there for a semester, but yet to honor him that way really is special,” Kent Landry said. “And I think it speaks to the sense of family and community that Texas State has.”
